newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Governor says Zaire army has duty to evict Tutsis.
newsitem.headline: Governor says Zaire army has duty to evict Tutsis.

text.p: Zaire's regional administrator who gave about 200,000 ethnic Tutsis one week to leave eastern Zaire said on Wednesday the army had a duty to evict Tutsis.
A government spokesman, however, played down the deadline by South Kivu Deputy Governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji, who accused the Banyamulenge Tutsis of destabilising the region.
"We are virtually in a state of war," Lwabanji told Reuters by telephone from the provincial capital Bukavu. "The Zaire army has a duty fight to safeguard our territorial integrity."
Aid workers said on Wednesday they feared all-out war in eastern Zaire after a one-week ultimatum from Zairean authorities for an estimated 200,000 ethnic Tutsis to leave.
State radio said Zaire's army chief of staff General Eluki Monga and senior military aides had travelled to the area "to assess the situation prevailing over there".
Government spokesman Boguo Makeli said the ultimatum announced by Lwabanji was a regional matter.
"There has not been a formal government declaration in this regard. To my knowledge the government has not yet issued an ultimatum to the Banyamulenge," he said.
"It's true that we all want the Banyamulenge to leave, but up to now the government has not spoken of one week," he added.
Zairean doctors said on Wednesday Banyamulenge rebels killed a total of 34 patients and six staff at a hospital Lemera, another town on the volatile border with Rwanda.
Two doctors told reporters in Bukavu that 100 Banyamulenge militiamen arrived at the hospital and attacked for eight hours.
The doctors said the Banyamulenge attacked because the hospital was treating Hutu war wounded from the conflict between the Zairean army, Banyamulenge and local Zairean tribes.

Conflict between the army and estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge has been growing for months. The Banyamulenge are ethnic Tutsis who arrived up to 200 years ago from what are now neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.

The conflict has been fuelled by the influx of more than one million Hutu refugees who fled civil war in their country in 1994 in which Hutus are accused of massacring up to a million minority Tutsis or their Hutu sympathisers.
